title: Ademe Detsi
author: Soyoqour Quarcoo Tchire
desc: Leaves washed in brine and stirred into boiling water for two minutes to maintain the green colour, then stirred fifteen minutes until the mixture becomes firm.
longDesc: Ademe is jute leaf — the same plant as the north's ayoyo and Nigeria's ewedu — and the Ewe make it into ademe detsi with crabs, smoked fish and fresh scallops. The two useful instructions are both about handling: wash the leaves in brine, and add them to boiling water stirring for two minutes to maintain the green colour. The sauce cooks about ten minutes, the seafood goes in, and then it is stirred with a wooden spoon for about fifteen minutes and gradually until the mixture becomes firm. No quantities are published, which is stated rather than filled in.
ingredients: Celery seed (nkitinkiti) — see the note on this identification
// No quantities are published in the source. See the note.
equipment: Bowl of brine, for washing the leaves
steps: Wash the ademe leaves in brine.
Add the leaves to boiling water and stir for 2 minutes, to maintain the green colour.
Make the sauce with the onions, tomatoes, garlic, ginger, celery seed and kpakpo shito, and cook about 10 minutes.
Add the meat, crabs, smoked fish and scallops.
Stir with a wooden spoon for about 15 minutes.
Stir gradually until the mixture becomes firm.
Serve with hot akple (GHA042), banku (GHA041) or kokonte.
chefTips: Wash the leaves in BRINE, not plain water. It is the only source in this collection that specifies salted water for jute leaf and it helps hold the colour.
Two minutes' stirring in boiling water to maintain the green colour. Longer and ademe goes olive-grey.
Until the mixture becomes firm is the finishing cue, after about fifteen minutes of stirring. Jute soup thickens as the mucilage develops.
Fresh scallops — adode — alongside crabs and smoked fish is a distinctly coastal Ewe combination and not something you see in the northern ayoyo.
Palm oil is optional here, which is unusual for a Ghanaian soup and makes this a lighter dish than most.
The source names nkitinkiti as celery seed; another Ewe cook names the same word as aniseed. The two are not the same spice and no source reconciles them.
No quantities exist in the source at all — not even 'a handful' for anything but the leaves. Build it by eye.
commonMistakes: Washing the leaves in plain water.
Boiling the leaves longer than two minutes.
Serving it thin, before it has firmed.
Adding palm oil heavily, which weighs it down.
Assuming nkitinkiti is aniseed when this source says celery seed.
sources: Adapted from 'Ademe Soup' in the 'Chopology' series, Ghana Broadcasting Corporation online, 29 April 2022. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Soyoqour Quarcoo Tchire'.

Ingredients exactly as printed, and NOTE THAT NONE CARRY QUANTITIES except the leaves: 'A handful of Ademe leaves'; Palm oil (optional); Garlic; Ginger; 'Celery seed (nkitinkiti)'; Onions; Tomatoes; Smoked fish; Crabs; 'Fresh scallops (adode)'; Kpapko shito — spelling as printed; Salt to taste. The ingredient list above reproduces that and carries a header saying so.

Method, step numbers confirmed across two fetches: wash the leaves in brine; 'add leaves to boiling water and stir for 2 minutes to maintain green color'; sauce 'Cook for about 10 minutes'; add the meat, crabs, fish and scallops; 'Stir with wooden spoon for about 15 minutes'; 'Gradually stir until mixture becomes firm'.
THE TWO CUES, both quoted: 'stir for 2 minutes to maintain green color' and 'Gradually stir until mixture becomes firm'. The second is a real endpoint.
THE COMMUNITY, quoted: ademe soup is 'one of the favorite soups of the people of the Volta Region'. Served with 'hot akple, banku, or kokonte'.

A SECOND EWE VERSION, with full quantities but no method, published at GHA089's sources rather than here: Fafa Gilbert, 'The Healthiest Molokhia/ Ademe/ Ewedu/Jute Soup Recipe Ever', 23 April 2019. Its ingredients, TWO-PASS: 1kg of picked fresh Ademe / Molokhia leaves; 1kg of Smoked or Grilled Tilapia or Mackerel; 500g of Smoked Barracuda (known as Lizzy); 150g of smoked dried Herrings or powder (Optional); 300g of fresh Crabs; 150g of smoked Prawns/Shrimps or 300g of fresh Prawns; 700ml of Water; 1 large sliced Onions; 1 Habanero chilli or 10 green Pettie Belle chillies (Kpakposhito); 1 teaspoon of Bicarbonate Soda or Akaun (Optional); Salt to taste. Spice blend: 20g of Ginger; 1 large Onion; 1 Habanero chilli; 1 teaspoonful of Aniseed (Nkitinkiti); 2 cloves of Garlic. ITS METHOD IS VIDEO ONLY. Her framing is useful: 'The Ewe tribe of Ghana and Togo do make Ademe Detchi or Dessi with the leaves and the Northerners of Ghana do use it making Tuo Zaafi.'
A SPICE DISAGREEMENT, unreconciled: nkitinkiti is 'Celery seed' on this GBC page and 'Aniseed' in Fafa Gilbert's list. Those are different plants and neither source explains the other.

A SOURCE REJECTED: Eat with Afia's vegetarian ademe detsi, byline 'support', a tofu-and-miso adaptation. Its one quotable cultural line is recorded: 'Ademe Detsi roughly translates to jute mallow soup in the Ewe language. Traditionally it is made with a base of fish and seafood flavoured with fermented locust beans (dawa dawa/iru), fermented fish...' SINGLE-PASS.
THE SAME LEAF, THREE REGIONAL NAMES: ademe to the Ewe, ayoyo in northern Ghana (GHA074), ewedu in western Nigeria. All are Corchorus — jute mallow — and all are wanted for the same slipperiness.
NO YIELD is printed. The five servings above is editorial.
healthBenefits: Jute leaf is exceptionally high in vitamins A, C and E, calcium, iron and folate.
Crabs, scallops and smoked fish together give a very complete amino acid profile.
The mucilage is a soluble fibre.
Optional palm oil makes this one of the leanest Ghanaian soups.
culturalNote: That the same jute leaf is ademe to the Ewe, ayoyo in the north and ewedu in Nigeria, and that all three traditions prize exactly the same slipperiness, is one of the clearest threads running across West African cooking. The Ewe version is the most seafood-heavy of the three, which is what you would expect from a coastal people.
